claims.text: Reducing the number of constituents in Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni-derived FCC alloys induces variations in short-range chemical order.
Variations in short-range chemical order govern the mechanical-property differences among these alloys.
Enhanced short-range order increases local barriers to dislocation motion.
Increased barriers to dislocation motion produce higher yield strength.
Enhanced short-range order modifies ductility relative to the equiatomic quinary alloy.
The investigated equiatomic quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys can be processed into single-phase FCC structures through controlled thermomechanical treatments.
Identical thermomechanical and aging conditions can provide comparable grain structures and phase stability across the composition series.
The relevant structural mediator is short-range chemical-order clustering within the FCC matrix.
Short-range-order-induced localized lattice barriers impede dislocation motion.
Compositions with reduced short-range order offer less resistance to dislocation glide.
Alloys with enhanced short-range order will have higher yield strengths than the identically processed equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni baseline.
Alloys with enhanced short-range order will exhibit altered ductility or strain-hardening behavior relative to the quinary baseline.
Alloys with diminished short-range order will have lower yield strengths than the quinary baseline.
The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy processed under identical conditions is the experimental performance benchmark.
The proposed mechanism is limited to single-phase FCC alloys within composition and processing windows that preserve phase stability.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to multiphase or significantly segregated alloys.
